entry.title: Antibes - An Unexpected Journey
entry.content:
📖 For readers unfamiliar with Chinese culture: We strongly recommend you read the Peach Blossom Spring to fully immerse yourself in this story.

Antibes was never in the plan. This was supposed to be a coastal trip heading east from Arles,1 starting in Cannes, threading through Nice, Monaco,2 Ventimiglia, spanning the entire Côte d’Azur.3 SNCF’s4 regional pricing brought the toll down to a minimum: thirty-five euros for three days, fifty for seven. If you were willing to practice a few rusty phrases of French with the elegant ladies past fifty at the platform ticket counter, you could save the two-euro card fee from the self-service machine — a broke exchange student’s indignity doesn’t end at the boarding pass paired with economy class in the terminal;5 you must also hoard every coin like the Dutch and the Vlaamse,6 or when nature calls in France, that cash-only pay toilet becomes your true reckoning.

Antibes entered the plan because my attitude toward travel has always been cautious. Before setting out, while drafting the itinerary, I compared prices carefully, from Charolais steak7 to Airbnb8 rentals; I collected my French friends’ experiences and noted the one-star reviews on Trip.com. I finally saw something in Cannes’s prices. I knew the Palme d’Or was awarded here, knew those directors and stars walked the red carpet toward eternity or oblivion, knew the name Théâtre Claude Debussy9 was itself an expensive ticket. But the festival’s glow has nothing to do with tourists, just as fireworks have nothing to do with the ragpicker. Cannes in May belongs to the stars; the rest of the year belongs to the landlords. I had fantasized about lying in a Cannes King’s Bed watching the coastline churn in the distance, but the Canopy10 price tag flashed its reply: you leave, the dream stays.

So I stopped fantasizing and chose Antibes. Beyond its three one-Michelin-star restaurants,11 lodging options were ample. My spending appetite swelled with U.S. equities.12 Abandoning my habit of sorting by price ascending, I found a charming and cheap place on Airbnb’s Guest-favorite list; for the first time booking in France, someone saw my East Asian face and replied in his mother tongue. I paid for that bargain soon enough. Lime e-bike13 could only park at the foot of the hill; the apartment, like a mansion in Beverly Hills,14 sat five hundred meters away and about fifty meters up on the Av. de la Rostagne. My French host, nearing sixty and about to retire, heard I had a lab meeting15 starting soon. He came up smiling, helped me wrestle the Wi-Fi into acceptable latency, and set out hand-ground coffee. His English carried the same estrangement as my four months of French, but that didn’t stop him from asking eagerly whether that Michelin lunch was to my taste.

“You’re quite well-informed, you know. During the Palme d’Or festival, they don’t stay in Cannes — they stay at my place.”

This was a ground-floor apartment16 hidden on the hillside above the coast, wrapped by an enormous terrace. No sea view, but tropical plants everywhere; when the wind rose, you could smell the Mediterranean. Its refinements didn’t end at the terrace, which seemed longer and more winding than my own fate. My wallet, pressed by European labor costs, drove me to cook for myself on every trip to France — or at least heat up American-style microwave cuisine. But this kitchen, larger than my loft17 living room, had every pot and utensil imaginable, four grades of salt, let alone those bottles and jars of Eastern spices. I thought of that coffee shop in Hangzhou: a three-group La Marzocco18 boiler steaming its mist onto the mugs overhead, sunlight refracting spectra onto their surfaces — world landmarks and scripts in every language, narrating backpackers’ travels across the globe in the tremor of steam. Here, fridge magnets swarmed over three doors. At the junction between upper and lower compartments: the Golden Gate Bridge.19 That place I once ached for, on the other side of the earth, was already the past.

Stunned by the Côte d’Azur × the Alps, I decided to unseal a forgotten Tour de France20 of my own. Limited by time and budget, I could only purchase a three-hundred-minute LimePass. At eight, just as the sky brightened, I slung my camera over my shoulder and rode downhill. At first the path was narrow, jolting over city tracks. Another half kilometer and I reached the coast — suddenly, the world opened wide. Antibes’s coastline is split by a spike of a peninsula: to the west, Juan-les-Pins21 looks out at the bustle of distant Cannes; to the east, the Baie des Anges22 is the Antibes that visitors come to see. My lodging was only five hundred meters from Juan-les-Pins, so naturally I followed the paradigm of this trip — head east, riding the peninsula’s hills deeper into the Mediterranean.

I wasn’t the only early riser. An Englishman with a Manchester accent jogged with his dog; now and then, road cyclists — solo or in clusters — screamed past on the opposite lane. As luck would have it, the coastal ride ended at the entrance of some luxury hotel: a construction vehicle straddling the road with a terse French sign informed all comers the way was closed. Every alternate route climbed. I had neither the stamina to scale mountains, nor thousands euros for a carbon-fiber bicycle, nor insurance good enough to summon a helicopter if things seems off. The green Lime e-bike, conspicuously out of place, was already the optimal solution. Still, climbing, I had to grumble: capped at twenty-five, the horsepower was simply not enough.

The itinerary was grand. The noble Liu Ziji of Nanyang never found the Peach Blossom Spring,23 yet I found Antibes without searching. The Alps unfolded at a turn. Nearby, the sea didn’t require swimming to reveal its deep blue, mirroring cerulean sky and white cloud under the subtropical high. In the distance, that had to be Nice: the airport awaiting a descending Emirates A380,24 four Rolls-Royce engines burning Middle Eastern oil money that might as well be free, their roar splitting the sky ahead of the enormous wake turbulence, announcing the arrival of this aerial colossus born in a factory in nearby Toulouse.25 On the other side of the airport, travelers were flying toward the future. My mind drifted back to Nyingchi at Tibet: a thirteen-year-old boy gazing down at the Yarlung Tsangpo River, looking up at the triangle of Namcha Barwa Mountain, golden. Before reaching Cairo or the British Museum, this was my pyramid. I held up my phone, the Alps and the Mediterranean shared the frame. A plane inched across the Live Photo. I thought of sending it to someone but locked the screen instead.

“To be honest, I’ve always believed my hometown is the best place in the world.”

Two weeks earlier I had reunited with a friend in Paris; for the first time I learned where he lived. When I mentioned my upcoming Côte d’Azur trip, he revealed his hometown lay right on the France-Italian border. He was Italian, yet carried none of the theatrical Italian accent; his hand gestures might even be fewer than mine. Last year, bored in class, he had been drilling Duolingo26 to get acquainted with Paris in advance. He failed some courses, yet his quirky ideas bursting out as an American across the Atlantic. I once told another Italian friend that “GPA cannot quantify a person’s intelligence, execution, or talent”27 — he was the living proof. One’s soil shapes one’s soul. Alfonso Cuarón’s28 Roma ends with a plane roaring in the distance over Mexico’s turmoil; someone who grew up twenty years on the Côte d’Azur may have drawn nourishment from the world through Nice airport. As for me, about to visit Monaco and a small Italian border town — beyond stockpiling anecdotes for future dinners and drinking sessions with friends, I was also doing it so that, two days later, the travel record on my DS-16029 would feed through the network into every immigration officer’s brain, and keep my U.S. visa from falling prey to Trump’s30 latest One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

Before my Cantonese flip-flops could be fully eroded by waves and sand, I made it back to the host’s place in time. He was busy on the phone while minding a child — his own or a friend’s, I couldn’t tell. I scrambled to pack, tossed winter clothes still damp into the dryer for an emergency tumble, and just managed to gather my bags before eleven, ready to head for Monte Carlo.31 The host’s call wasn’t finished, but he came to the door anyway to shake my hand goodbye — parting felt exactly like meeting.

Tao Yuanming had already imagined such an otherworld. The people of the Peach Blossom Spring — “they knew nothing of the Han dynasty, let alone the Wei or Jin”32 — embodied the earliest utopia.33 My first-year Chinese teacher in middle school loved to banter. He spoke of his old days in the state system: first, two weeks to crush the final exams, then a whole month on The Peach Blossom Spring — riffing from the year 42134 all the way to the French Revolution.35 I never once heard him teach that text. My actual middle-school Chinese teacher, heavy with banwei36 rushed through the essay. All I remember: “Memorize the full text, spot check next week.” The story sank like that, until I came to Leuven37 — the Eurostar38 shook me toward Paris at three hundred kilometers per hour, and the vertigo was overwhelming before the Louvre’s39 free, all-encompassing embrace. Along the Grande Galerie,40 near-ten-meter canvases unfurled the French Revolution: from Napoleon’s coronation41 to La Liberté guidant le peuple.42 Under Delacroix’s43 brush, the goddess of Liberty strides barefoot over the barricade, hoisting the tricolor — the French from then on wore freedom on their bodies; the Peach Blossom Spring still gathered dust in a middle-school textbook corner. Ten years later the realization hit: that Chinese class was my Enlightenment.44

The next stop was Monte Carlo, and I had missed it, lost in memory. Google Maps45 flickered through the Schengen Area46 and Monaco, briefly losing signal, and only after stepping out of Monaco’s dim station — built inside a mountain cave47 — did I realize I had overshot. Halting French and an intermittent map signal led me to a village station. I pulled out my phone album. The location pin read: Carnolès.48

The platform was empty. Just me, my oversized red Grand Frais shopping bag, and a ticket machine that may or may not take credit cards.

Four years ago, that platform wasn’t empty. Hangzhou. A metro station I’d transferred through five hundred times. Every minute accounted for, and still I missed the connection. She said she’d wait outside the convenience store at West Lake Cultural Square station. The store had a floor-to-ceiling glass wall. She leaned against it, head down, looking at her phone. From a distance I saw a purple silhouette, brown hair pinned with a black butterfly clip. Couldn’t be sure it was her. I slowed my steps, walked to the glass door, and sent her a message telling her to turn around. Four months later she told me she’d spotted me long before that.

The platform across from Carnolès stood bare. Four years ago she saw me through the glass; I didn’t see her. Now there’s nothing on the other side, and I see it perfectly.

I first encountered this story’s title in the subtitle of the first Hobbit film:49 Bilbo Baggins, content in Bag End, has his life upended by a wizard and dwarves, and sets off on an unexpected journey. Tolkien50 wrote a book out of it; mine fills only these three pages.

The westbound train came quickly. On the Côte d’Azur, trains depart as densely as Hangzhou Metro Line 5.51 When I was six, my father gave me a hardcover world atlas. Beneath the worn laminate was the origin of my world geography. Late at night, after lights-out, I taught myself to use a calculator, worked out GDP per-capita for over two hundred countries, and reached a conclusion: the world’s richest people live in Monaco. From that small room, I walked twenty years. I walked here.

Xinyu(Christopher) Yang, Night of February 15, 2026
Written in the first snow of Leuven

Disclaimer: This work was co-created with Claude-Opus-4.6

  1. Arles — an ancient city in southern Provence, France, on the banks of the Rhône, famous for Van Gogh’s residence and work there. ↩

  2. Monaco — a microstate in southwestern Europe, surrounded on three sides by France, bordering the Mediterranean to the south. The world’s second-smallest country (after the Vatican), known for extreme wealth. ↩

  3. Côte d’Azur — the Mediterranean coast of southern France, renowned for sun, beaches, and the resort life. ↩

  4. SNCF — Société Nationale des Chemins de fer Français, the French National Railway Company. ↩

  5. Terminal refers to the airport departure hall; intra-EU flights are almost exclusively narrow-body, direct, and all-economy. ↩

  6. Vlaamse refers to the Dutch-speaking region of Belgium; Dutch-speakers are stereotypically tight with money, as evidenced by the phrase “going Dutch.” ↩

  7. Charolais steak — Charolais cattle originate from Burgundy in east-central France, pasture-raised year-round. Unlike the richly marbled Japanese Wagyu familiar to most Chinese diners, Charolais is lean with very little fat, yet extraordinarily tender, carrying a deep, robust “beefy” flavor — a prestige ingredient in fine French restaurants. ↩

  8. Airbnb — a short-term rental platform where hosts rent rooms or entire homes to travelers. ↩

  9. Théâtre Claude Debussy — the main venue of the Cannes Film Festival, where the red carpet and premieres take place. ↩

  10. Canopy — the Canopy by Hilton hotel brand, luxury four-star hotel. ↩

  11. Michelin star — a restaurant rating system; “one star” typically means “worth a visit,” up to a maximum of three. ↩

  12. U.S. equities — the American stock market. ↩

  13. Lime App; in French, lime is commonly called citron vert (“green lemon”). ↩

  14. Beverly Hills — the affluent enclave in Los Angeles, shorthand for “where the mansions cluster.” ↩

  15. Lab meeting — common academic jargon for a research group’s regular internal discussion. ↩

  16. In Europe, floors are counted from zero; the ground floor corresponds to the first floor in China. ↩

  17. Loft — an open, high-ceilinged living space. ↩

  18. La Marzocco — an Italian high-end commercial espresso machine brand, common in specialty cafés. “Three-group” refers to a top-tier commercial model with three brew heads. ↩

  19. Golden Gate Bridge — the iconic suspension bridge in San Francisco. ↩

  20. Tour de France — the French bicycle race; used here to mean “traveling by bike through the land, Tour-de-France style.” ↩

  21. Juan-les-Pins — a seaside town on the Côte d’Azur, administratively part of Antibes. ↩

  22. Baie des Anges — French for “Bay of Angels,” the bay near Nice. ↩

  23. From Tao Yuanming’s “The Peach Blossom Spring.” Liu Ziji was the last person to seek the hidden utopia; he never found it. After him, no one asked the way again. ↩

  24. A380 — the Airbus super-jumbo jet (Airbus A380). ↩

  25. Toulouse — a city in southwestern France and the site of a major Airbus final assembly plant. ↩

  26. Duolingo — a language-learning app. ↩

  27. GPA — Grade Point Average, used to measure academic performance. ↩

  28. Alfonso Cuarón — Mexican director, two-time Oscar winner for Best Director (Gravity and Roma). ↩

  29. DS-160 — the U.S. online nonimmigrant visa application form (for tourist visas, student visas, etc.). ↩

  30. Trump — Donald Trump, President of the United States. ↩

  31. Monte Carlo — Monaco’s most famous district, renowned for its luxury casino, high-end hotels, and the Formula 1 Grand Prix. ↩

  32. From The Peach Blossom Spring: the villagers, having fled the wars of the Qin dynasty, were so isolated they had never heard of the Han, much less the Wei or Jin. ↩

  33. Utopia — an imagined ideal and perfect society. ↩

  34. The year 421 (Yongchu 2, Southern Song dynasty) — when Tao Yuanming composed The Peach Blossom Spring. ↩

  35. The French Revolution (1789–1799) — the bourgeois revolution in France that overthrew absolute monarchy, rallying under the banner of “Liberty, Equality, Fraternity,” widely regarded as foundational to the world’s democratic systems. ↩

  36. Banwei — Chinese internet slang for the weary, numb, rule-following aura office workers acquire from years of high-pressure work. ↩

  37. Leuven (also spelled Louvain) — a city in the Dutch-speaking region of Belgium, about 20 km northeast of Brussels, home to KU Leuven. ↩

  38. Eurostar — the high-speed cross-Channel train linking London with Paris and Brussels. ↩

  39. The Louvre (Musée du Louvre) — in central Paris, originally a royal palace, now a museum; free for EU youth under 26. ↩

  40. The Grande Galerie inside the Louvre, home to masterworks including La Liberté guidant le peuple. ↩

  41. The Coronation of Napoleon (Le Sacre de Napoléon) by Jacques-Louis David, depicting Napoleon’s 1804 self-coronation at Notre-Dame. The canvas is nearly ten meters long. ↩

  42. La Liberté guidant le peuple (Liberty Leading the People), set against the July Revolution of 1830. ↩

  43. Eugène Delacroix — 19th-century French Romantic painter, creator of La Liberté guidant le peuple. ↩

  44. The Enlightenment — the 17th–18th-century European intellectual movement championing reason, liberty, and equality. ↩

  45. Google Maps — the most commonly used navigation app for overseas travel outside China. ↩

  46. The Schengen Area — the zone of European countries that have abolished mutual border checks under the Schengen Agreement, allowing free movement. Monaco, though not a Schengen member, is entirely surrounded by France and maintains open borders. ↩

  47. Gare de Monaco-Monte-Carlo — to conserve the principality’s scarce land, the entire station is built underground in tunnels and rock caverns, with perpetually poor lighting. ↩

  48. Carnolès — a small train station in southeastern France near the Monaco border. ↩

  49. The film’s original title: The Hobbit: An Unexpected Journey. ↩

  50. Tolkien — J. R. R. Tolkien, English author. ↩

  51. Hangzhou Metro Line 5 — a metro line running through several central districts of Hangzhou, with extremely high ridership and dense departures during rush hour. ↩

entry.title: Verhoogde Tegemoetkoming(Increased Reimbursemnet)
entry.content:
0. Introduction

For international students arriving in Leuven, Vlaams, Belgium, navigating the healthcare system might feel less like ordering your daily coffee and more like waiting for your slowest firend to finish their fries - it would takes patience, paperwork and more than a little frustration. The good news is, Belgium boasts one of Europe’s most affordable healthcare systems; The bad news is, it also has bureaucracy thick enough to put your patience thorugh the ultimate test. Unlike in the US, you won’t face bankruptcy from medical bills here, but uninsured visits to the ER or the GP can definitely leave your wallet feeling lighter.

Speaking from my personal experience —— having spent ~1k euros due to misunderstandings, wrong insurance choices, and uninsured medical visits —— I learnt the hard way. So let’s talk about what might just be the most valuable aspects of Belgium’s welfare system:

Verhoogde Tegemoetkoming

Below are guidance mainly summarised and generated by GPT-5-pro via web research, and I made modifications based on its output.

What is “Verhoogde Tegemoetkoming” (VT)?

Belgium’s “you-earn-less-so-healthcare-costs-you-less” status. If you have VT, doctor visits, meds and hospital stays are way cheaper - in gerenal speaking, it will be ~70% less than typical insurance and ~95% less than uninsured case; you only pay the copay (e.g., visit GP is €0-1). Think of it as a discount card issued by your health fund.

Of course there’s an income limit for qualifying as “low-income”(somewhere ~2200 euros/month, price differs based on your marital status). Most students not juggling a full-time job shouldn’t worry about crossing that threashold.

A pretty nice video intro by @Amal explains it neatly, and how you could get VT step-by-step.

1. What VT changes within the Health Insurance

We will only cover the case w/ CM(Christelijke Mutualiteit) —— the insurance provider I’m familiar with because, well, that’s the one I’ve got.

Searching for geconventioneerd(Contracted) Provider

Short version: Think of geconventioneerd(Contracted) as the Belgian health-care equivalent of a fixed-price lunch menu —— no unpleasant surprises at checkout. Prices are regulateed and renegotiated every two years by RIZIV(Belgium’s social security), keeping healthcare affordable. There are 3 types of Conventioneringsstatus(Contracting Status) you should be noticed:

  • A geconventioneerd doctor sticks to the official RIZIV tariffs;
  • A Gedeeltelijk geconventioneerd(partially contracted) one follows the menu except during their self-declared “surcharge hours” - you can find this information on RZIZV site;
  • A niet geconventioneerd(non-contracted) provider makes up prices à la carte.

Here’s how to check a provider’s status in 60 seconds:

  1. Open RIZIV’s SilverPages search: https://webappsa.riziv-inami.fgov.be/silverpages/.
  2. Search by name, Berop(Occupation), Conventioneringsstatus(Contracting Status) or any other section.
  3. If it’s Gedeeltelijk geconventioneerd, make sure to click on provider’s Uren wel/niet geconventioneerd(Contracted and non-contracted hours) to see the exact time for that.

To put it simple: always searching for geconventioneerd or gedeeltelijk geconventioneerd: they are covered by insurance.

GP consultations (geconventioneerde GP)

  • You pay only the small co‑pay (remgeld); the rest is billed to the fund via the third‑party payer. VT patients have a right to this at the GP. (RIZIV)

  • Examples:

    • GP consult with GMD (globaal medisch dossier): €1.00 remgeld with VT (vs €4.00 without VT).
    • GP consult without GMD: €1.50 remgeld with VT (vs €6.00 without VT). (CM)

Psychological care (two layers)

  • Publicly funded first‑line psychology (RIZIV networks): for adults ≥24 y the personal share is €4 perSta session with VT (vs €11). See CM’s explanation of network‑based care. (CM)
  • CM’s extra member benefit (outside the network): CM refunds part of sessions with recognised clinicians; for children & youth CM states 50% up to €30 per session, or 75% up to €45 per session if you have VT (up to lifetime caps). (CM)

Medicines & contraception

  • VT leads to higher reimbursement across many reimbursable medicines (lower remgeld). RIZIV confirms an extra reimbursement for contraceptives for people ≤24 years or with VT regardless of age/gender (morning‑after pill is reimbursed for everyone). (RIZIV)

Hospitalisation: lower personal shares + CM top‑ups for VT

  • RIZIV confirms that a patient’s personal share (co‑pay) depends on status, and VT reduces what you pay. (RIZIV)
  • CM details the fixed hospital forfaits where VT pays less or nothing; e.g., forfait medical imaging co‑pay is €1.98 with VT (vs €6.20), forfait technical procedures per admission is €0 with VT, and per‑day hospital medicines forfait is €0 with VT. (CM)
  • CM extra support if you have VT and no hospital insurance: CM pays 75% of the legally defined personal shares (room, medical/paramedical fees, and top‑ups on reimbursable medicines). This is a CM‑specific complementary benefit. (CM)

Maximumfactuur (MAF): yearly cap on copay

  • Belgium’s Maximumfactuur(Maximum Amount) caps a family’s annual co‑pays; with VT you benefit from the “social MAF” at a lower cap. For 2025, social MAF is €527.27; if a chronic‑care trigger is met, the cap drops to €410.10 (HZIV)
  • General info pages on MAF from Vlaanderen.be and CM explain how caps apply and that VT households can be treated as a separate “VT‑sub‑family” for the social MAF. (Vlaanderen.be)

2. Other VT perks you’ll appreciate

Public transport (student‑relevant)

  • De Lijn (Flanders): with VT you are entitled to a reduced‑rate annual pass (Buzzy Pazz 6–24y or Omnipas 25–64y). Discount is applied automatically when buying/renewing online or at a point of sale (they check your VT via the national register). De Lijn’s pages list the VT discount and automatic processing. (De Lijn)
  • NMBS/SNCB (trains): VT holders get 50% off standard tickets with the VT discount (via a specific entitlement loaded and checked at purchase). See NMBS’s discount overview and the “Large families, persons …” page on how the VT entitlement is verified. (NMBS announced a new fare structure earlier in 2025, but as of 30 Sep 2025 the official discount page still lists 50% for VT holders—check at purchase in case of updates.) (Belgian Train)
  • MIVB/STIB (Brussels): VT holders can buy the RVV pass at a reduced price—€8.10 per month or €85 per year (2025 page). (STIB - MIVB)

Flemish “zorgpremie” (care premium) of the Vlaamse Sociale Bescherming

  • If you had VT on 1 Jan of the previous year, you pay the reduced zorgpremie. In 2025 the standard premium is €64; with VT it’s €32. (The Flemish government has indicated a general increase from 2026; but 2025 values are as stated here.) (Departement Zorg)

Leuven‑specific municipal benefits connected to VT

  • Free UiTPAS (kansentarief) + 80% discount on partner culture/sport/leisure activities and membership/registration fees across Leuven, Bierbeek, Herent, Oud‑Heverlee. The city explicitly lists this under VT.
  • Free annual package of household waste bags if you have VT (city measure; see the Leuven page for details and the 2025 council decision).
  • The Leuven VT page also points to De Lijn/NMBS VT transport discounts, local support (e.g., energy coaching) and “Iedereen Verdient Vakantie” discounted trips.

Telecom/internet (important nuance)

  • Since 1 Mar 2024, Belgium runs a new “Sociaal internetaanbod”. Having VT by itself does not make you eligible (eligibility is based on other social criteria); official guidance is explicit on this point. (Economie)

3. Special offers & KUL-student‑oriented extras

UiTPAS Leuven kansentarief

  • With a recent attest VT, Leuven grants a free UiTPAS and 80% discounts on tickets, membership and course fees at participating organisations in Leuven/Bierbeek/Herent/Oud‑Heverlee; great for cinema, community sports, cultural venues, workshops. See examples and application steps (accepts a VT attest not older than 3 months; annual auto‑renew where still eligible).

KU Leuven Sport – (partial) reimbursement via your mutuality

  • CM’s sports‑club benefit: up to €15 per person per year for membership at a sports club, sports centre/service, recognised jogging or swimming initiations, etc. You can apply this to (part of) your KU Leuven Sports Card or fitness subscription. (CM)
  • KU Leuven Sports publishes the mutuality forms and explains the one‑time yearly reimbursement process (get the right CM form, have KU Leuven Sport stamp it, and submit to CM). (KU Leuven)

CM student travel assistance for study abroad (Erasmus, etc.)

  • If you’re studying in another European country, CM’s student travel assistance gives access to the Mutas emergency centre and reimbursement for urgent medical costs abroad (complements your European Health Insurance Card). Notify CM before you go. (CM)

A few other CM extras students often use

  • Vaccinations: certain vaccines are reimbursed by the compulsory insurance and CM; CM also documents travel‑vaccine reimbursements pathways (and via optional CM MediKo Plan). (CM)
  • Eye care: if there’s no statutory reimbursement, CM pays €40/year towards a new pair of glasses as a member benefit (separate from optional insurances). (CM)

Quick how‑to (claiming the main benefits)

  1. Check/obtain proof of VT In Mijn CM or request an Attest verhoogde tegemoetkoming (CM forms). You’ll need this for UiTPAS, sometimes for transport products. (CM)

  2. Use the third‑party payer at the GP As a VT patient, your GP must apply it; you pay only the remgeld (e.g., €1 with GMD). (RIZIV)

  3. Psychological care Prefer RIZIV network psychologists when possible (co‑pay €4 with VT), and use CM’s extra refunds where applicable (youth: up to 75%/€45 with VT). (CM)

  4. Public transport

    • De Lijn: buy or renew your Buzzy Pazz/Omnipas; the VT discount is applied automatically online once your national number is entered. (help.delijn.be)
    • NMBS: ensure your VT entitlement is recognised at a ticket office or in your online profile to get 50% discount on tickets. (Belgian Train)
    • MIVB: buy the RVV subscription (listed price: €8.10/month or €85/year). (STIB - MIVB)

  5. UiTPAS (Leuven region) Apply online or at a sales point with your VT attest (<3 months old) to get a free card and 80% discounts at partner organisations.

  6. KU Leuven Sports Card reimbursement Download CM’s sports reimbursement form, get it stamped at KU Leuven Sport, and submit to CM (up to €15/year). (CM)

  7. Keep an eye on your annual cap If your remgeld reaches the MAF cap (with VT usually €527.27 in 2025), the rest of that year’s eligible co‑pays are reimbursed automatically. (HZIV)

I use GPT-4.5 to polish the article, and base on the number of grammar mistakes in my posts, you can tell how much it has been involved.
entry.summary: All you need to know about Verhoogde Tegemoetkoming

entry.title: Pitch For Thesis Topic
entry.content:
I would like to start with describing my thesis project, and this will be the one that I intend to pitch, despite I haven’t started to work on it yet.

It’s about devloping a classification algorithm based on pharmarcy dispensing records, and we focus on one-specific type of disease – diabetes patients.

Outlet Choice

Let’s suppose this research project has been successfully completed, and the corresponding essay has been published after harsh peer review. Now, We aim to share this work with the general public.

The first one to reach out will be Casey Ross, a reporter with special focus and specialize in health AI. He cares about the AI safetly and real-world impact on care delivery, which makes him a perfect initial contact as we try to expand my research to clinicians and policy makers through his report.

Message Box

  • Issue: The current approach to diabete care is passive, only addressing problems after they have already developed.
  • Problem: Diabete Patients record are heterogenous, i.e. every patient is unique.
  • Benefits: This allows doctors to give personalized care to the patients who need it most before they get sicker.
  • So what: Fewer emergency room visits, saving money for the government and improve the quality of life for patients.
  • Solution: We use novel modelling technqiues to predict their future behavior, based on pharmarcy records.

Pitch Email

Dear Casy Ross,

We are researchers from KU Leuven and Itec-imec. Your insightful coverage in patient care resonates deeply with a critical issue in diabetes management: a one-size-fits-all approach that too often leads patients into costly complications.

Our recent study offers a way to preempt this. By digging into underutilized pharmacy dispensing records w/ novel survival tree models, we can track each patient’s adherence trajectories over time.

This isn’t just another predictive model — it’s a validated method to identify and intervene with the highest-risk patients before hospitalization becomes necessary. It offers a concrete step beyond today’s current, reactive approach.

You can find details on this website:

  • xxxxxxxxxthere-is-supposed-to-be-a-websitexxxxxxxxxxx .

We have a summary and are willing to discuss w/ you how this approach could rewrite the playbook for managing chronic disease.

Thank you for considering our work and looking forward to your reply.

Best regards,

Xinyu Yang

Challenges

This may face follwing criticism:

  • Classified as spam email, and be ghosted. No reply at all.
  • “This sounds like more AI hype. We see dozens of these ‘predictive model’ papers. What makes this one different?”
  • “What’s truly novel about the methodology? Others have used machine learning on diabetes data for years.”
  • “How reliable is pharmacy dispensing data? It doesn’t capture everything, and patients could just be stockpiling medication.”

entry.title: Knowledge Distillation: putting AI Giants in Your Pocket

link.title: Knowledge Distillation: putting AI Giants in Your Pocket

entry.content:
Introduction

Imagine you’re a great chef :cook: with a special recipe you’ve worked on for many years. Your helper wants to learn from you, but the recipe is complicated. Instead of teaching every tiny step, you share the main points in a simple way. This approach to teaching complex concepts is similar to what we call model distillation in Artificial Intelligence (AI).

Just as alcohol distillation isn’t about reducing volume, but about purifying a substance, model distillation isn’t simply shrinking models, but a process of extracting and transferring knowledge.

Why is Model Distillation Important?

Most AI models are huge, with trillions (like millions of millions) of parameters. These big models, like the ones used for apps like ChatGPT, are very smart but difficult to run on regular laptops because they need a lot of power. Model distillation lets us shrink these big models into smaller ones that can run easily on everyday devices.

Don't be fooled by size!

In the left picture, we can see
  • The teacher model is Deepseek-R1-0528, one of the frontier models.
  • The distilled model is Deepseek-R1-0528-Qwen3-8B, being 100 times smaller than the teacher model, and can be deployed in a PC.
  • Despite being significantly smaller, Deepseek-R1-0528-Qwen3-8B still achieves good performance, even compared to other frontier models.

Also, because the student model is small, it needs much less electricity to think(great for the earth!). Smaller also means cheaper, so more people can play with it on laptops and even cellphones instead of mega-servers that cover areas comparable to football stadiums.

Knowledge Distillation Process

How Does Large Model Distillation Work?

It's inspired by the chemical distillation process and has the following parallel relationship:

  • Chemical distillation: :test_tube: Mixed substance → :fire: Heating → :dash: Vaporization → :snowflake: Cooling → :droplet: Pure liquid
  • Model distillation: :teacher: Large model → :gear: Training → :bulb: Knowledge extraction → :arrows_counterclockwise: Conversion → :student: Small model

Here’s what it means for each step:

  • Teacher AI Model 🧑‍🏫: This is a big AI model, like ChatGPT, that knows a lot and gives very detailed answers.
  • Student AI Model 🎓: This is a smaller model made to work quickly on phones and computers.
  • Training and Knowledge Transfer 🔄: The teacher AI looks at lots of data and gives the correct answers and explains why these answers are correct.
  • Learning Process 📚: The student AI learns both the correct answers and the reasoning behind them. This helps the student AI give good answers even though it is smaller.

Take-away: Distillation is an Apprenticeship

Model distillation is like an apprenticeship, where the student learns directly from the teacher, step by step. Just as an apprentice chef learns cooking skills by watching and following closely as the experienced chef prepares dishes, the smaller AI model learns key concepts directly from the larger, knowledgeable AI model.

Conclusion

Through model distillation, we demonstrate a way to make Large AI models more accessible, efficient, and widely usable, not just those with access to massive computing resources.

entry.title: Analysis II Tutorial Notes
entry.content:
We choose to introduce metric spaces and normed vector spaces at the beginning of the course. Convergence is a concept that runs throughout all of analysis, and most convergence can be uniformly described using the language of metric spaces … This makes transitions to advanced topics such as continuity of multivariable functions, uniform convergence of function sequences, and even convergence in $\mathcal{L}^p$ spaces much more seamless. — Pin Yu

During the final semester of my undergraduate studies, I volunteered to tutor first-year students in Analysis. Instead of following the convoluted approach found in traditional Chinese textbooks, I presented these concepts through the lens of metric spaces. This perspective doesn’t add unnecessary abstraction, but rather provides clarity and unified approach.

Below are links to some of my previous tutorials (note: content is primarily in English with some Chinese, as it was developed for Chinese students):
